stem: A 54-year-old man with exertional chest pain undergoes coronary angiography, which reveals stenosis of all three major epicardial arteries.  Coronary artery bypass graft surgery is planned.  During the procedure, the surgeon intends to use the great saphenous vein as the graft to bypass the stenotic lesions.  Which of the following anatomic landmarks will be most useful for locating the proximal and distal ends of the vein?​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​

options.label: A
options.text: Lateral malleolus and anterior superior iliac spine

explanation:
Coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery sources healthy vessels from elsewhere in the body to bypass areas of atherosclerotic narrowing in the coronary arteries.  The left internal mammary (thoracic) artery located near the heart is commonly used, but additional vessels are often needed.  The great saphenous vein is the longest superficial vein in the body and is commonly harvested from the leg and thigh for grafting purposes.

The great saphenous vein originates from the medial aspect of the dorsal venous arch of the foot, passes anterior to the medial malleolus (medial ankle), and ascends up the medial aspect of the leg and thigh.  In the proximal anterior thigh, 3-4 cm inferolateral to the pubic tubercle, the great saphenous vein dives deep through the cribriform fascia of the saphenous opening to join the femoral vein.

(Choice A)  No veins course laterally from the ankle (lateral malleolus) to the pelvis (anterior superior iliac spine).  Penetrating injuries to the region below the anterior superior iliac spine could damage the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve of the thigh.

(Choice B)  The small (lesser) saphenous vein originates from the lateral aspect of the dorsal venous arch, passes posterior to the lateral malleolus, and ascends within the posterior leg to reach the popliteal fossa, where it empties into the popliteal vein.

(Choice C)  No major veins course from the medial malleolus to the popliteal fossa.  The posterior tibial vein courses from the plantar aspect of the foot to just inferior to the popliteal fossa, where it merges with the anterior tibial and fibular veins to form the popliteal vein.

(Choice E)  The popliteal vein courses from the popliteal fossa to the adductor hiatus, where it becomes the femoral vein.  The femoral vein then proceeds through the femoral triangle, where it receives the great saphenous vein before passing under the inguinal ligament to become the external iliac vein.

Educational objective:The great saphenous vein originates from the medial aspect of the dorsal venous arch of the foot, passes anterior to the medial malleolus, and courses superiorly up the medial leg and thigh to the femoral triangle, where it drains into the femoral vein a few centimeters inferolateral to the pubic tubercle.​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​
